items.title: Before You Write the Script, Ask Yourself This Question
items.summary: Do you know how long it takes to make a film? It’s, like, a really long process. It takes a long time. That is, if you’re doing it right from development to release. What does that mean? It means you might have an idea and not see it come to fruition for literal years. You’ll probably write several drafts, send it around for feedback, then maybe even put it on a shelf for a while. When the right moment arises, maybe you’ll pick it up again… and do more rewrites. Maybe you’ll get some interest. Maybe you’ll get some money. Only then will you start to think about preproduction, which if you’re an indie filmmaker is quite an involved process. As a writer, you might be asked to add new characters or change locations or cut things for budget. It’s a whole other ballgame. And that can take even more time. Screenwriter and novelist Matt Harry has published six novels, sold a TV pilot, and had a couple of low-budget screenplays produced. His fantasy young adult novel Sorcery for Beginners got optioned for TV by Boatrocker Media, the producer behind Apple's Palm Royale. His new dystopian detective novel Ash Land dropped in May from IFWG Publishing. In a recent Film Courage interview, Harry talked about what he's learned after 20-plus years of getting paid to write, including one lesson he wishes someone had drilled into him on his very first job. This is the question he now asks himself before starting any new idea, and the two-year cautionary tale that taught him why. - YouTube www.youtube.com This Question Might Save You Years We’ve already talked about how slowly things move when you’re a writer. But what does that mean for a career, and what should you ask going into a project? items.title: Avid Media Composer to Get Boost in Secure Collaboration Across Shared Storage Solutions
items.summary: Avid Media Composer is getting a boost as it aims to keep up with the competition and give its loyal user base new ways to move faster, collaborate more flexibly, and scale to the workflows modern teams need. The big news is that this release brings fully supported, secure collaboration across shared storage solutions with Media Composer Enterprise. The update is set to accelerate multicam editorial with PhraseFindAI Multicam AutoCut, plus add some other helpful features and workflow enhancements. Here’s everything you need to know about this latest Avid Media Composer update. Avid Media Composer Update 2026.8 Years go by, and Avid remains a solid, popular option for video editors looking to take on feature films or other content in today’s modern ecosystem. Still not quite at the footprint of Adobe Premiere or DaVinci Resolve, Avid has a loyal user base that remains active, and the company isn’t sitting idly by; it’s still pushing plenty of updates and innovation. This latest update is a good example of what Avid is trying to offer with Media Composer, adding new features to help editors move faster, collaborate more flexibly, and scale in ways modern teams need. Along with the new fully supported and secure collaboration across shared media solutions update, Avid Media Composer is also getting improved transcript control and new practical workflow enhancements that should reduce friction in everyday editing. Pricing and Availability Overall, this looks like a substantive update, with several new features and the removal of previous limitations on tracks and resolutions in Media Composer First, which gives aspiring editors a true no-cost entry point into the company’s professional editing platform. You can find more info on the different plans for Standard, Ultimate, and Enterprise on the company’s website here.

items.summary: Tim Curry died on Aug. 26. The actor became iconic several times over during his illustrious career, but it all started with an offbeat musical in which he played a lead part. Today’s quote comes from the 1975 film version of The Rocky Horror Picture Show, directed by Jim Sharman, from Richard O'Brien's 1973 stage musical. Curry played Dr. Frank-N-Furter, a role he originated on the London stage. The film served as his film debut. What an entrance. In the film, squeaky-clean engaged couple Brad (Barry Bostwick) and Janet (Susan Sarandon) get a flat tire in a storm and take shelter in a castle owned by Dr. Frank-N-Furter, a self-described "sweet transvestite from Transsexual, Transylvania," who's unveiling his lab-made creation, Rocky. They engage in seduction, murder, and an alien reveal. It’s a cult classic, one of cinema’s most iconic midnight movies. The music and lyrics were composed by Richard O'Brien in 1972, while the original musical arrangements are by Richard Hartley. The quote comes from a musical sequence near the end of the film, and it’s a five-world distillation of everything the character stood for. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Scene This song is part of a three-song medley called "The Floor Show." It happens near the end of the film, when Dr. Frank-N-Furter hosts a cabaret-style show. At this point, Frank has frozen his captives using his Medusa Tranquilizer. He unfreezes them, dresses them up, forces them into a cabaret in the RKO theater's pool, and leads the number that peaks on a refrain of "don't dream it, be it." Frank sings the opening, emerging from mist, clad in a corset and mink. He descends onto an extended diving board and leaps into the smoke below, where the pool is revealed. items.title: Iconic Villain Moment: Anton Ego - One Bite Changes Everything
items.summary: Ratatouille’s Anton Ego functions more so as a secondary villain on the sidelines for the majority of the film. It’s not until close to the third act that his minimal but brooding presence becomes important to the story and thematics of the film. But when it does, it changes everything. Let’s take a look at the seamless integration of Anton Ego’s character, and what it means for the film. Why He’s on the Sidelines The general theme for the antagonists of Ratatouille, whether it’s for Chef Skinner or Anton Ego, is jealousy and greed. Skinner throughout the film is desperate to make sure that Linguini doesn’t succeed in his new role at Gusteau’s restaurant, while also evading the revelation that he’s actually Gusteau’s son, and the sole heir to his fortune. Ego, on the other hand, is more interested in maintaining his reputation as the harshest, most trusted critic in town. And thanks to Skinner’s greed in the first two acts of the film, he entirely succeeds. No one knows the truth, Ego’s original review still stands, and no one is the wiser about their potential faults. His Grand Entrance ‘Ratatouille’Credit: Walt Disney Studios It’s not until Skinner’s deception is brought to light that Ego is forced to defend his reputation. With Remy and Linguini at the helm of the restaurant, business is booming. Much to Ego’s dismay. It’s clear in Ratatouille that when a character’s pride is threatened, no matter how superficially, they will do whatever it takes to make sure that it’s restored. Ego intimidates the staff at Gusteau’s and promises to be back, ready for an impossibly great meal. The Moment of Revelation The moment of truth for Ego’s character comes the moment he takes his first bite of the Ratatouille dish that Remy cooks for him. He is immediately transported back to his mother’s home cooking after a bike accident as a child. items.title: HUG-VIS: A Multimodal Benchmark for Human-centered Understanding and Generation in Visual Intelligence
items.summary: arXiv:2608.26517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visual intelligence seeks to perceive, interpret, and synthesize the visual world and is central to modern computer vision. Human-centered visual intelligence is especially demanding because it studies people as expressive, socially situated subjects whose meaning is rarely conveyed by appearance alone. It couples vision with audio and language across four representative tasks: human emotion recognition, human video generation, human voice cloning, and human video matting. Yet existing resources remain task-specific, providing modalities and annotations for individual problems rather than a shared foundation coordinating understanding and generation. This limits multimodal signal use and broader research. We address this gap with HUG-VIS, a unified benchmark for Human-centered Understanding and Generation in Visual Intelligence. It contains 8,400 seated half-body videos of 30 professional actors, each performing the same 280 emotion-action-prompt assignments under a controlled Mandarin studio protocol, with synchronized video, audio, text, and alpha mattes. We evaluate diverse open- and closed-source models across the four tasks under a unified zero-shot protocol using automatic metrics, criterion-specific mean opinion scores, and multiple cross-task analyses. Results show that (i) linguistic content dominates current emotion recognition, while purely visual affect recognition is weakest; (ii) in video generation and voice cloning, automatic metrics and human judgment agree overall but differ in their top rankings, requiring joint reporting; (iii) boundary fidelity under motion is the main remaining obstacle for human matting; and (iv) task difficulty varies across emotions, models, and metrics, with notable cross-task correlations. The dataset and results are available at https://github.com/GML-MMGroup/HUG-VIS.

items.title: Hyperspectral Diffusion Equivariant Imaging (HyDiff-EI): A Self-supervised Framework for Hyperspectral Image Inpainting
items.summary: arXiv:2608.26812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A novel Hyperspectral diffusion Equivariant Imaging (HyDiff-EI) framework for solving the hyperspectral image (HSI) inpainting problem has been presented here. Unlike conventional diffusion-based methods that rely on large-scale pretraining, HyDiff-EI is a test-time optimization framework that learns directly from a single corrupted HSI acquisition. This makes it flexible for different sensor configurations and particularly well-suited for practical remote sensing scenarios where large annotated hyperspectral datasets are limited. To address the ill-posed nature of unsupervised inpainting, we embed equivariant consistency constraints within the diffusion process. By leveraging the inherent geometric symmetries and intrinsic characteristics of HSIs, HyDiff-EI bridges the gap between generative diffusion modeling and self-consistent physical priors. We empirically show that coupling diffusion modeling with equivariant priors substantially enhances noise robustness and generalizability. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets including Chikusei, Botswana, and EMIT demonstrate that HyDiff-EI offers remarkable inpainting quality over existing self-supervised and diffusion-based algorithms in both noiseless and noisy cases.

items.title: Why Short Films Still Matter for Building a Writing Career
items.summary: This post was written by Dr. Bob Pondillo, Ph.D., Professor Emeritus—Media/Culture/Screenwriting. We are meaning-making, pattern-seeking, storytelling creatures. If you take nothing else from this column, remember that. THAT is the key that unlocks a writer's world. Storytelling and meaning-making are one of the human animal's evolved, innate abilities. It comes as standard equipment built right into our noggins. Think about that. How to tell and understand stories is hardwired in our brains, like language and walking! AND story infrastructures are found everywhere. Its frameworks are always resident in novels, newscasts, TV shows, movies, songs—and that scaffolding is constantly being reinforced in our media-drenched culture. Clearly, we've evolved to learn our world and understand our place in it through stories. That's why I used to tell my writing students, "If you can tell a joke, you already know the essential elements of any story, including screenplays." Simple, right? Right! Just not easy. But why isn't it easy? Well, I sense the primary reason is that most newer writers haven't yet awakened to a story's hidden structures, methods, and conventions. Okay, so how does one awaken and gain access to such seemingly indiscernible structures? Oh, that's the easy part because they're not indiscernible. They're right there before us, always teaching and bolstering what you already know. So just pay attention and become a friggin' monkey! Now I don't mean you need to swing from trees and eat bananas. I mean it in the sense of the old bromide, "Monkey see, monkey do." Y'see, every good movie, TV show, series, novel, or joke is instructing you. Every time you read a book or watch a moving image, you're learning exactly how to build the story you have in your heart. So, pay attention as you read, study as you watch, and, like any smart monkey, copy THAT! Just don't throw any shit at your audience. items.title: Lock in On Your Edits With These Focus-Ready Sony Headphones
items.summary: We've all been there: you're looking to edit a project for a client or for yourself, and you're ready to lock in and focus up, but distractions come around. items.title: The Best War Movies Boomers Grew Up Watching
items.summary: I am not a boomer; I am very much a millennial, but I grew up with Boomer parents, and one of my fondest memories is sitting on the couch next to my old man and watching whatever war movie was on TNT on a Saturday afternoon. If you didn't know, the Baby Boomer generation was born between 1946 and 1964, and war movies were a staple of weekend matinees, drive-in theaters, and late-night television broadcasts for them. They were called the Baby Boom because of the GIs who returned from WWII and Korea and started families. They came of age during the Vietnam War and have seen other massive moments in history. So what are the war movies that defined their eras and that bring them back for more? Let's dive in. The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957) - YouTube www.youtube.com Director: David Lean Writer: Carl Foreman and Michael Wilson (based on the novel by Pierre Boulle) Cast: Alec Guinness, William Holden, Jack Hawkins, Sessue Hayakawa This is the ultimate Saturday afternoon movie. I can hear the rain falling down and then see the opening credits playing. Suddenly, we're in a Japanese POW camp in Burma, where British prisoners are forced to construct a vital railway bridge for their captors. The officers look on, taking pride in their work and hoping that the building of the bridge will keep them alive. The iconic "Colonel Bogey March" whistle will live in your ears forever. The Great Escape (1963) - YouTube www.youtube.com Director: John Sturges Writer: James Clavell and W.R. Burnett (based on the book by Paul Brickhill) Cast: Steve McQueen, James Garner, Richard Attenborough, Charles Bronson, James Coburn This is one of the greatest movies of all time. If I see it on TV, I have to stop and just watch from whatever point we're at. It's a lesson in futility and ingenuity. The whole story is based on true events during WWII in a prison camp where POWS are trying to escape via a tunnel. The whole movie is three hours of tension. items.title: How Different Is ‘Rear Window’ From the Original Short Story?
items.summary: Rear Window (1954) is one of the best films directed by Alfred Hitchcock, and it’s ranked among the greatest films of all time. But what screenwriter John Michael Hayes did shouldn’t be overlooked. Hayes expanded on the setup and characters of the original short story by Cornell Woolrich — Grace Kelly wouldn’t have even had a role if the film was a truly faithful adaptation. Find out below what stayed the same and what changed in Rear Window. The Short Story That Became a Hitchcock Film Rear Window isn’t the only adaptation made from the work of prolific crime writer Cornell Woolrich. Additional short stories of his that were turned into films include: “The Boy Who Cried Murder,” which was made into the 1949 noir The Window, and “The Bride in Black,” which was made by director François Truffaut. ‘Rear Window’ (1954)Credit: Paramount Pictures Still, the short story that inspired Rear Window is what Woolrich’s is best known for. Under the pseudonym William Irish, Woolrich wrote “It Had to Be Murder,” back in 1942, with a plot that Rear Window fans would recognize. A man named Hal Jeffries is unable to leave his apartment due to a broken leg. He becomes a nosy neighbor by the window, but his observations take a dark turn when he believes Lars Thorwald, who lives in the building across, has killed his sickly wife and is actively covering it up. Jeffries alerts two allies to his theory. The sleuthing culminates in Thorwald trying to kill Jeffries, but failing. That sounds all familiar, doesn’t it? While the screenplay for Rear Window doesn’t pivot into new directions that completely revise the plot, they do stand apart in the changes put in. There is Daphne du Maurier’s Rebecca and The Birds, Patricia Highsmith’s Strangers on a Train, and there is Woolrich’s story.
